title: Could This Be a Pre-Order of a Search Tree?

concept.title: Keep a stack of the road to the right; a value may never go below a bound you have passed
body: A list of different numbers is given. Is it the **pre-order** list (node, left subtree, right subtree) of some binary search tree? Building the tree is not necessary: the pre-order list of a search tree has a strong structure that a **stack** can check in one pass.

Read the numbers left to right. A number smaller than the previous one is the left child of the previous one (the road goes left), so push it. A number **larger** than the stack top is a right child of some earlier node: pop the stack while the top is smaller than the number; the last popped value is then the node whose right child this number is, so from now on **every later number must be larger than that node** (everything after the right child lies in the right subtree). That is a lower bound `low`.

body.code:
low = -infinity
stack = []
for x in a:
    if x < low:                      # it would have to be in an already closed left part
        print("no")
        break
    while stack and stack[-1] < x:
        low = stack.pop()            # we moved into the right subtree of this node
    stack.append(x)
else:
    print("yes")

body: Every number is pushed once and popped at most once, so the check is O(n). The bound `low` only ever increases, which is what makes the single pass enough.

statement: Given `n` different integers, decide whether they are the pre-order list of some binary search tree (the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree; in a search tree every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger). Print `yes` or `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of values.
The second line has `n` different integers.
constraints: -10^9 <= every value <= 10^9, and all values are different

examples.note: It is the pre-order of the tree with the root 8, left subtree 5 (children 1 and 7) and right child 10: yes.
After 9 (which is larger than 8, so it belongs to the right subtree of 8) the number 7 cannot follow: no.

hints: Use a stack for the nodes whose right subtree has not started yet.
When a number is larger than the top of the stack, pop while the top is smaller; remember the last popped value as a lower bound.
If a later number is smaller than the lower bound, the answer is no.

explanation: A stack keeps the nodes whose right subtree has not started. A larger number pops the smaller tops, and the last popped value becomes a lower bound that every later number must exceed.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

low = -10 ** 18
stack = []
valid = True
for x in a:
    if x < low:
        valid = False
        break
    while stack and stack[-1] < x:
        low = stack.pop()
    stack.append(x)
print("yes" if valid else "no")
